newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Skoda profit seen burdened by deals.
newsitem.headline: Czech Skoda profit seen burdened by deals.

text.p: Analysts worry that Czech machinery giant Skoda a.s. strapped on too heavy a load when it concluded acquisitions of controlling stakes in two troubled truck-makers -- Tatra a.s. and Liaz a.s..
They say the deals will drag down otherwise healthy consolidated results for 1996.
The company forecast unconsolidated gross profit at 600-700 million crowns ($21.6-$25.2 million) for last year on turnover of 27 billion crowns.
Ondrej Datka OF Patria Finance sees the consolidated gross profit to take a large hit from the truck deals.

"We expect Skoda to record 300-350 million crowns pre-tax profit in 1996, including Liaz's and Tatra's losses, which will reduce Skoda's consolidated (gross) income by an estimated 400-500 million crowns," Datka said.
Consolidated 1996 net profit of Skoda, based in the western city of Plzen and not affiliated with the car maker now owned by Volkswagen AG, is seen at zero to 100 million crowns.
"In concrete terms we expect (net consolidated) profit at about 80 million crowns," said Petr Hajek at Zivnostenska Banka.
For 1995, Skoda posted a consolidated loss of 432 million crowns on sales of 21 billion.
Skoda holds a 52 percent stake in Liaz and 43 percent in Tatra. The management of Skoda has said the two truck-makers should be profitable in 1997, but analysts are sceptical.
"The management's plans in the truck-makers seem to be too optimistic. We expect to see them out of red numbers as late as 1998," Martin Mottl, an analyst from Brno Broker Group, said.
Skoda's low basic capital, which creates a high ratio of indebtedness, seems to be a problem especially for the further development of the company, analysts said.

"Looking at the balance sheet of the consolidated results for the first three quarters of 1996, (Skoda) seems to be over-indebted," said Jiri Mensik from CSOB. "The level of indebtedness of total assets is 54 percent, and the ratio of liabilities to own capital is 126 percent."
Skoda has hinted it is considering raising basic capital, but that could not come until after the second half of 1997.

"Because the shares can't be sold under par when issued, we can expect that the price of 1,000 crowns per share will become a new psychological boarder," Blanka Houhova, an analyst from BH Securities, said.
"The price of shares should not drop under (par), once the decision to raise of the basic capital is taken," she said.
At midday in the Wednesday session of the Prague Stock Exchange, Skoda shares were trading at 998 crowns, five lower than Tuesday's close.
Most analysts recommend a short- to medium-term hold on the stock, but longer-term prospects are still seen as positive.
"I think that by the end of 1997 the price could be over 1,300 crowns," Tomas Navratil from AKRO Capital said.
